terms.short: The 1960s shift to youth-driven, mod fashion led by the miniskirt and designers like Mary Quant.
terms.definition: In the 1960s fashion's center of gravity moved from couture houses dressing mature elites to the youth market and the street, an upheaval the press called the "Youthquake." London designer Mary Quant championed the miniskirt and playful, affordable mod styles aimed at young women, while André Courrèges advanced a parallel space-age modernism in Paris. Bold geometric prints, bright colors, flat shapes, and synthetic materials suited a generation defined by pop music and consumer freedom. Fashion became a vehicle for youthful rebellion and identity rather than a top-down dictation of taste.
terms.example: Mary Quant's miniskirt, sold from her London boutique Bazaar, made the hemline a symbol of 1960s youth liberation and shifted fashion's authority from the couture salon to the street.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("Mary Quant")

terms.short: The postwar American movement that made New York the center of avant-garde painting.
terms.definition: Abstract Expressionism arose in New York in the 1940s and 1950s as the first American movement to win international influence, marking the shift of the art world's center from Paris to New York. It is loosely split into gestural "action painting," in which Jackson Pollock dripped and poured paint onto canvases laid on the floor to record physical movement, and "color field" painting, in which Mark Rothko and Barnett Newman used large, simplified expanses of color to evoke contemplation and the sublime. The work was typically large in scale, abstract, and concerned with the act of painting and raw emotional or existential content. Critics like Clement Greenberg championed its emphasis on flatness and pure abstraction. It defined the postwar avant-garde and provoked the reactions that followed.
terms.example: Pollock's Autumn Rhythm (Number 30) (1950), an all-over web of poured and flung skeins of paint with no focal point, embodies action painting as a record of the artist's movement across the canvas.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: Communal ritual and choral dance in ancient Greece, including the singing-dancing chorus at the heart of tragedy.
terms.definition: In the ancient Greek world dance (orchesis) was inseparable from religion, festival, and theater rather than an autonomous stage art. The chorus in Athenian tragedy and comedy moved as a singing, dancing collective in the orchestra, the circular dancing-floor named for the activity itself. Plato discussed dance as moral education in the Laws, and writers distinguished forms such as the dignified emmeleia of tragedy and the wild sikinnis of satyr plays. Dance also served Dionysian and other cult worship, binding the community through shared rhythmic motion. The art was understood as mimesis — bodily imitation of character and emotion — laying a conceptual foundation later European theater dance would revisit.
terms.example: The chorus of Sophocles' or Aeschylus' tragedies sang and danced their odes in the orchestra of the Theatre of Dionysus, the movement of the group physically articulating the play's emotional commentary.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Early-20th-century composers abandoned the tonal system, through atonality and serialism on one side and rhythmic primitivism on the other.
terms.definition: In the first decades of the 20th century, the long expansion of chromatic harmony reached a breaking point and composers stepped outside traditional tonality. Arnold Schoenberg moved from free atonality to the twelve-tone technique, a method that orders all twelve chromatic pitches into a row to organize music without a tonal center, joined by his pupils Berg and Webern in the Second Viennese School. On a different front, Igor Stravinsky exploded rhythm and tonal expectation through pounding irregular meters and harsh dissonance. Together these innovations shattered the common-practice assumptions that had governed Western music since the Baroque.
terms.example: The 1913 Paris premiere of Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring, with its violent rhythms and dissonance, provoked a near-riot in the audience and became the emblematic scandal of musical modernism.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 4; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'atonality'

terms.short: The critical idea that the director is the true author of a film, stamping even studio work with a personal vision.
terms.definition: Formulated by the young critics of Cahiers du cinéma — notably François Truffaut's polemic against a 'cinema of quality' — the politique des auteurs argued that the best films bear the recognizable signature of their director rather than their screenwriter or studio. It elevated Hollywood craftsmen such as Hitchcock and Hawks, finding consistent themes and style across their filmographies. Imported to American criticism by Andrew Sarris as 'auteur theory,' it reframed film history around directors as artists. The idea underwrote the director-driven movements that followed and still shapes how films are canonized and marketed.
terms.example: Treating Alfred Hitchcock's thrillers as a single body of work — recurring motifs of guilt, voyeurism, and the wrong man, told in an unmistakable visual style — exemplifies reading the director, not the studio, as the film's author.
terms.source: Andrew Sarris, Notes on the Auteur Theory; François Truffaut, A Certain Tendency of the French Cinema (Cahiers du cinéma); Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction

terms.short: The Enlightenment reform that made ballet a self-sufficient dramatic narrative told through expressive movement rather than ornament and convention.
terms.definition: By the mid-eighteenth century reformers argued that ballet should tell a coherent story through pantomime and expressive dancing instead of serving as decorative interludes in opera. Jean-Georges Noverre crystallized this program in his Lettres sur la danse et les ballets (1760), demanding dramatic truth, the abolition of cumbersome masks and stiff costumes, and dance that conveyed real emotion and action. The resulting ballet d'action treated the whole ballet as a unified drama, anticipating the later integration of story and movement. Contemporaries such as Gasparo Angiolini in Vienna pursued parallel reforms, and Noverre's ideas spread across Europe through his appointments and writings. This is the conceptual hinge on which ballet became an independent narrative art.
terms.example: Noverre's Lettres sur la danse (1760) argued for ballet as expressive drama, and his stagings such as Médée et Jason aimed to move audiences through pantomimic action rather than mere virtuoso display.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: French court ballet under Louis XIV, where Beauchamp's codification of the five positions turned aristocratic spectacle into a formal technique.
terms.definition: The ballet de cour was the grand French court entertainment of the seventeenth century, fusing dance, music, poetry, and elaborate staging in spectacles in which the king himself performed. Louis XIV, who danced the title role in the Ballet de la nuit (1653) and was nicknamed the Sun King after it, made ballet an instrument of royal prestige. In 1661 he founded the Académie Royale de Danse, and his dancing master Pierre Beauchamp is credited with codifying the five fundamental positions of the feet that still anchor ballet technique. Jean-Baptiste Lully supplied much of the music and the comédie-ballet collaborations with Molière. This royal institutionalization moved ballet from the ballroom toward the professional proscenium stage.
terms.example: In the Ballet de la nuit (1653) the young Louis XIV appeared as the rising sun, the performance that helped earn him the title Sun King and cemented ballet as a tool of absolutist display.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Diaghilev's itinerant company that detonated ballet into modernism, fusing radical choreography, music, and design into avant-garde theater.
terms.definition: Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, based in the West from 1909 and never performing in Russia, transformed ballet into a laboratory of modernist collaboration. Choreographers Michel Fokine and then Vaslav Nijinsky broke with academic convention — Fokine's Schéhérazade and The Firebird, and Nijinsky's angular, anti-balletic works. The company's commissions united composers such as Igor Stravinsky, painters such as Picasso, and designers in a total-artwork synthesis. The 1913 premiere of Nijinsky's choreography to Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring provoked one of the most notorious riots in performance history. Later choreographers including Léonide Massine and the young George Balanchine passed through the company, which seeded ballet companies across Europe and America after Diaghilev's death in 1929.
terms.example: The 1913 Paris premiere of The Rite of Spring, with Stravinsky's dissonant score and Nijinsky's stamping, turned-in choreography, set off a near-riot in the theater and announced ballet's entry into the modernist avant-garde.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Lavish 17th-century dress under which France, led by Louis XIV's court, became fashion's arbiter.
terms.definition: Baroque dress favored abundance — billowing silks, cascades of lace, ribbons, and rich trimmings — expressing the grandeur of absolutist courts. Under Louis XIV, France deliberately built fashion into an instrument of state and economy, promoting domestic silk and lace and turning Versailles into the style center of Europe. The mantua, a looser gown draped and pinned over a stiff bodice and petticoat, emerged late in the century and reshaped women's dress. Court etiquette dictated dress in fine gradations, and changing seasonal styles began to spread through prints and dressed dolls, an early fashion-information system.
terms.example: Louis XIV's Versailles made lace, ribbons, and the formal grand habit de cour compulsory court dress, deliberately steering taste so that France — not Spain or Italy — set Europe's rules.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: The Baroque era replaced modes with functional major-minor tonality, anchored by basso continuo and dramatized by the concerto.
terms.definition: Around 1600 the modal world gave way to functional tonality, a system of major and minor keys organized around the pull of dominant to tonic that would govern Western music for roughly three centuries. Performances were underpinned by basso continuo, a bass line with a keyboard or lute player realizing harmonies from figured-bass shorthand. New instrumental genres flourished, above all the concerto, which set a soloist or small group against a larger ensemble in a ritornello structure. Antonio Vivaldi standardized the three-movement solo concerto and wrote hundreds of them, fixing the form's fast-slow-fast template.
terms.example: Vivaldi's The Four Seasons (1725) is a set of violin concertos with descriptive sonnets, an early high point of program music that vividly maps tonality and ritornello form onto images of nature.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 2; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'concerto'

terms.short: Turn-of-the-century elegance defined by the S-bend corset and Poiret's loosening of structured dress.
terms.definition: Belle Époque and Edwardian dress favored an opulent, mature silhouette: the so-called health or S-bend corset thrust the bust forward and hips back, paired with frothy lace, pastel tea gowns, and elaborate hats. From around 1908 Paul Poiret challenged this structure, promoting higher waistlines and softer, columnar gowns that reduced corseting, drawing on Orientalism, the Ballets Russes, and bold color. His harem trousers, hobble skirts, and turbans dramatized a new exoticism in fashion. The period marks the transition from the rigidly engineered Victorian body toward the looser lines that would define modern dress.
terms.example: Paul Poiret's circa-1908 high-waisted gowns and vivid Orientalist designs began dismantling the S-bend corset, freeing the waist and pointing fashion toward the unstructured 20th-century body.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("Paul Poiret")

terms.short: The sacred image tradition of the Eastern Christian world, built on gold grounds and fixed conventions.
terms.definition: Byzantine icon painting produced devotional images of Christ, the Virgin, and the saints on wood panels, in mosaic, and in fresco, governed by theological convention rather than naturalistic observation. Figures are frontal, elongated, and flattened against shimmering gold-leaf grounds that signified divine, placeless light; reverse perspective and hierarchic scale subordinated the natural world to the spiritual. The tradition survived the Iconoclastic controversy of the 8th–9th centuries, which debated whether sacred images were licit, and afterward codified its visual language. Icons were understood not as portraits but as windows to the holy, venerated as conduits to their prototypes. This style shaped medieval Christian art across the Mediterranean and into Italy.
terms.example: The 6th-century encaustic icon of Christ Pantocrator at Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, shows the frontal, two-sided face and gold-flecked solemnity that defined the type for a millennium.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; R. Cormack, Byzantine Art

terms.short: The Baroque drama of stark light cutting through deep shadow, pioneered by Caravaggio.
terms.definition: Chiaroscuro is the modeling of form through strong contrasts of light and dark; in its extreme Baroque form, tenebrism, Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio (1571–1610) plunged his scenes into near-total darkness pierced by a single raking light. This theatrical illumination heightened emotional and spiritual drama and pulled sacred events into a gritty, immediate, often plebeian present, with unidealized figures observed from life. Caravaggio's realism and stagecraft spread rapidly, inspiring a generation of followers — the Caravaggisti — across Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, and France. His method made light itself a narrative and dramatic instrument. It became a defining device of seventeenth-century painting.
terms.example: The Calling of Saint Matthew (c. 1599–1600) in San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome, sends a diagonal shaft of light across a shadowed tavern to single out the tax collector at the instant of his summons.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: Cervantes's parody of chivalric romance, often called the first modern novel.
terms.definition: Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) published Don Quixote in two parts (1605, 1615), telling of an aging gentleman so steeped in chivalric romances that he sets out to revive knight-errantry. By colliding his deluded idealism with mundane reality — and pairing him with the earthbound Sancho Panza — Cervantes turned parody into a profound study of illusion, perspective, and the gap between books and the world. Its self-aware play with narration, including characters who have read Part One, anticipates later metafiction. It is widely regarded as the foundational work of the European novel.
terms.example: Don Quixote charges a row of windmills, convinced they are giants — an image so durable that 'tilting at windmills' became shorthand for noble, deluded struggle against the imaginary.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to Spanish Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Coco Chanel's jersey, simplicity, and the 1920s flapper that redefined the modern liberated woman's dress.
terms.definition: Gabrielle "Coco" Chanel built modern womenswear on comfort, simplicity, and borrowed menswear ease, using soft jersey (previously an underwear fabric) for relaxed suits and dresses. In the 1920s the fashionable silhouette dropped the waist, shortened hems, and abandoned the corset for a slim, boyish flapper line suited to dancing and movement. Chanel popularized the chic, versatile little black dress and costume jewelry, making understated elegance a deliberate style rather than a sign of poverty. This shift mirrored women's expanding social freedom after the First World War and made practicality fashionable.
terms.example: Chanel's 1926 little black dress — simple, short, and endlessly wearable — was hailed as a fashion "uniform," embodying the 1920s ideal of the active, unencumbered modern woman.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("Coco Chanel")

terms.short: Chaucer's pilgrimage frame-tale that established Middle English as a literary medium.
terms.definition: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) wrote in the London Middle English of his day, lending it lasting literary prestige. The Canterbury Tales frames a storytelling contest among pilgrims of every social rank traveling to Thomas Becket's shrine, allowing Chaucer to move freely among genres from courtly romance to bawdy fabliau. His sharply individualized portraits in the General Prologue — the Wife of Bath, the Pardoner, the Miller — give an unmatched cross-section of medieval society. His ear for irony, character, and colloquial speech anticipated the realism of later English fiction.
terms.example: The Wife of Bath's Prologue runs far longer than her tale, as she defends her five marriages and her appetite for mastery — an early instance of a vivid speaking voice overwhelming the story it was meant to introduce.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of English Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Orson Welles's 1941 debut, a landmark that fused deep focus and fractured chronology into a new expressive maturity for the medium.
terms.definition: Directed by and starring the 25-year-old Orson Welles, Citizen Kane traces a newspaper magnate's life through the conflicting memories of those who knew him. With cinematographer Gregg Toland, Welles pushed deep-focus photography so that foreground and distant background stayed simultaneously sharp, letting a single shot stage layers of meaning. The film told its story out of order through overlapping flashbacks, used low angles and ceilinged sets, and layered overlapping sound. Often cited atop critics' polls, it became shorthand for cinema's coming-of-age as a director's art.
terms.example: The deep-focus shot in which young Charles plays in the snow far outside the window while, indoors and close to camera, his mother signs him away — keeping both planes sharp — lets a single frame hold the boy's loss and the adults' decision at once.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; British Film Institute (BFI) Sight and Sound; The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: The Greco-Roman foundation (~800 BCE–500 CE) that bequeathed proportion, mimesis, and the canon of genres to every later art.
terms.definition: Classical Antiquity is the shared Greco-Roman wellspring the Western arts return to again and again. Greece formulated ideals of proportion, harmony, and mimesis (imitation of nature) and invented the dramatic genres of tragedy and comedy; Rome inherited, monumentalised, and transmitted them. Across forms the period sets first principles — the Homeric epic for narrative, the modal system for music, drapery and the idealized body for the visual arts, ritual and choral movement for dance. Later eras define themselves largely by how they revive or rebel against this canon.
terms.example: When Renaissance humanists 'rediscovered' antiquity, they were reaching back to this hub — Vitruvian proportion in architecture, classical metre in poetry, the contrapposto stance in sculpture — proving the era functions as a reference point the whole timeline orbits.
terms.source: Gombrich, The Story of Art (Greek & Roman art); The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica (Classical antiquity)

terms.short: Greek and Roman dress built from draped, uncut rectangles of cloth rather than tailored garments.
terms.definition: Classical dress was fundamentally untailored: rectangular lengths of wool or linen wrapped, pinned, and belted on the body rather than cut and sewn to fit. Greeks wore the chiton (a tunic fastened at the shoulders with fibulae) under the himation (a draped mantle), while Roman citizens marked status with the toga, a large semicircular wrap reserved for free men. Color, fineness of weave, and the breadth of a purple stripe (clavus) encoded rank far more than cut did. The aesthetic ideal was the fall and flow of fabric over the body, an ideal repeatedly revived whenever later fashion looked back to antiquity.
terms.example: The Roman toga praetexta, bordered with a purple stripe, signaled magistrates and freeborn boys; its sheer unwieldiness made it ceremonial dress, the visible badge of citizenship.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: The vertically integrated American film industry that, from the late 1920s, mass-produced genre pictures and manufactured movie stars.
terms.definition: The arrival of synchronized sound with The Jazz Singer (1927) transformed the business and craft of film almost overnight. A handful of major studios — MGM, Warner Bros., Paramount and others — controlled production, distribution, and exhibition, running directors, writers, and contract actors like a factory. This system standardized the conventions of continuity editing and clear, goal-driven storytelling and organized output by genre: the Western, the musical, the gangster film, screwball comedy. It also engineered the star system, building actors into bankable public personas. Antitrust rulings and television eroded the model after the 1940s.
terms.example: Casablanca (1942), assembled on Warner Bros.' lot from contract talent and standing sets, embodies the studio system: a genre romance polished to invisible craft, anchored by stars the studio itself had made.
terms.source: Bordwell, Staiger & Thompson, The Classical Hollywood Cinema; Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; British Film Institute (BFI)

terms.short: The grand classical ballet perfected at the Imperial Russian theaters by Marius Petipa, codifying the full-evening, multi-act ballet spectacle.
terms.definition: In the later nineteenth century the center of ballet shifted to Imperial Russia, where the French-born ballet master Marius Petipa raised the classical full-length ballet to its highest formal development. Working at the Mariinsky in St. Petersburg, Petipa structured grand multi-act ballets balancing narrative pantomime, the formal pas de deux, and large symmetrical corps de ballet ensembles. His collaborations with composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky produced The Sleeping Beauty (1890) and, with Lev Ivanov, the definitive staging of Swan Lake (1895), while The Nutcracker (1892) rounded out the canon. Petipa codified the architecture — entrée, adagio, variations, coda — that still governs classical ballet. This Russian classicism became the technical and repertory foundation for twentieth-century ballet worldwide.
terms.example: Swan Lake, restaged in 1895 by Petipa and Lev Ivanov to Tchaikovsky's score, fixed the white-act swan corps and the dual Odette/Odile ballerina role as touchstones of classical ballet.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The plural landscape of today's theatrical dance and the global rise of street and hip-hop dance from urban vernacular roots.
terms.definition: Contemporary dance names the eclectic post-1960s theatrical practice that absorbs ballet, modern, postmodern, and global influences without a single fixed technique. Choreographers such as Pina Bausch, with her genre-blurring Tanztheater, William Forsythe, who deconstructed ballet's geometry, and Twyla Tharp, who fused idioms, exemplify its range. In parallel, street dance emerged from African-American and Latino youth culture: breaking (b-boying), locking, and popping grew alongside hip-hop music in 1970s New York and on the West Coast. These vernacular styles spread worldwide through media and battles and entered the concert stage and even the Olympics, with breaking debuting as a competition event in 2024. The era is defined by hybridity and the erosion of any boundary between high-art and popular dance.
terms.example: Breaking, born among youth in the Bronx in the 1970s alongside hip-hop music, traveled from street battles to global stages and made its Olympic debut at the Paris 2024 Games.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The radical fracturing of form and viewpoint that remade twentieth-century painting.
terms.definition: Cubism, developed by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in Paris from around 1907–1908, abandoned single-viewpoint perspective by analyzing objects into faceted geometric planes seen from multiple angles simultaneously, flattening and fragmenting space. The early Analytic phase reduced subjects to monochrome shards barely legible against their grounds; the later Synthetic phase reassembled them from flatter shapes, brighter color, lettering, and pasted papers (collage and papier collé). Cézanne's structural analysis and the abstraction of African and Iberian sculpture were key catalysts. Cubism overturned the Renaissance window onto reality and reconceived the canvas as a constructed object. It became the pivotal language from which much of modern abstract art descended.
terms.example: Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907), with its angular, mask-like faces and shattered, contradictory space, is the proto-Cubist rupture that announced the dismantling of traditional representation.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: Dante's visionary epic of the afterlife, which made vernacular Italian a literary language.
terms.definition: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) composed the Divine Comedy in the Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin, helping establish Italian as a language of serious literature. The poem narrates the pilgrim's journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, guided first by Virgil and then by Beatrice, in a tightly engineered structure of terza rima and one hundred cantos. It fuses Christian theology, classical learning, and contemporary Florentine politics into a single cosmological design. Its scope and moral architecture made it the supreme literary achievement of the late Middle Ages and a bridge toward the Renaissance.
terms.example: At the gate of Hell, Dante reads the inscription warning all who enter to abandon hope, then descends through nine circles where each punishment mirrors the sin — fortune-tellers walk with heads twisted backward, having claimed to see ahead.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to Italian Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Christian Dior's 1947 collection that revived the cinched waist and full skirt after wartime austerity.
terms.definition: In 1947 Christian Dior launched a collection whose nipped waist, padded hips, and long, full skirt the press dubbed the "New Look," reversing the boxy, fabric-saving styles of the war years. It restored an emphatically hourglass, ultra-feminine silhouette built on internal structure — boning, padding, and yards of cloth — and reasserted Paris couture's authority after the disruption of occupation. The look was both celebrated as glamorous renewal and criticized for its extravagance and return to restrictive shaping. It dominated the 1950s and set the template for the decade's elegant, structured femininity.
terms.example: Dior's 1947 "Bar" suit — soft-shouldered jacket over a full pleated black skirt, waist sharply cinched — defined the New Look and made Paris the postwar arbiter of glamour once more.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("Christian Dior")

terms.short: ~1750–1820: reason, clarity, and balance — Rococo's last sweetness giving way to Neoclassical order and the Classical style.
terms.definition: The Enlightenment prized reason, clarity, and balance. In music the Classical style (Haydn, Mozart, the young Beethoven) refined sonata form and public concert life; in painting, lighthearted Rococo yielded to the moral severity of Neoclassicism (David); in literature, satire (Swift, Voltaire) and the rising novel (Defoe, Richardson) addressed a literate middle class; ballet was reformed into expressive 'ballet d'action'; and dress moved from Rococo extravagance toward the restrained Neoclassical Empire line. Order, proportion, and the public sphere define the age.
terms.example: Mozart's symphonies and David's 'Oath of the Horatii' share one Enlightenment instinct — clarity of form and balanced structure standing in for reason itself — even as one is sound and the other paint.
terms.source: Gombrich, The Story of Art (Age of Reason); Taruskin, Oxford History of Western Music (Classical style); Encyclopædia Britannica (Enlightenment; Neoclassicism)

terms.short: The age of reason's weapon of choice — satire aimed at folly, vice, and superstition.
terms.definition: Enlightenment writers wielded satire to defend reason and expose hypocrisy across the long 18th century. In England, Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels and 'A Modest Proposal' used fantastic premises and deadpan irony to indict politics and inhumanity, while Alexander Pope's polished heroic couplets skewered literary and social vanity in works like The Rape of the Lock. In France, Voltaire's Candide demolished facile optimism through relentless catastrophe and the closing turn to cultivating one's garden. The mode prized clarity, wit, and moral correction over Baroque ornament.
terms.example: In 'A Modest Proposal,' Swift's narrator calmly recommends that the Irish poor sell their children as food — a monstrous suggestion delivered in the cool register of an economic pamphlet, so that the irony indicts the reader's own indifference.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of English Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: A late-1950s–1960s French movement of young critic-directors who made personal, formally playful films breaking classical rules.
terms.definition: Emerging from the critics of Cahiers du cinéma, the New Wave put theory into practice: cheap, fast, location-based filmmaking that prized the director's personal voice. Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless flaunted jump cuts and direct address; François Truffaut's The 400 Blows brought autobiographical tenderness and a freeze-frame ending. Drawing on Italian Neorealism's freedom and their own admiration for Hollywood auteurs, they treated film history as a living conversation, quoting and subverting it. Their lightweight cameras, improvisation, and self-aware style reshaped art cinema everywhere.
terms.example: The casual jump cuts in Godard's Breathless (1960) — splicing out moments within a single conversation in a moving car — announced that a film could openly show its own seams and still feel more alive, not less.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; Cahiers du cinéma; The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: A 1920s German movement that externalized psychological states through distorted sets, sharp shadow, and stylized design.
terms.definition: Emerging in the Weimar Republic, German Expressionist cinema treated the frame as a painted state of mind rather than a window on reality. The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) used jagged, hand-painted sets and skewed perspective to mirror its unstable narrator, establishing the movement's signature of décor-as-psychology. Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927) scaled the style up into a vast dystopian metropolis, and F.W. Murnau's Nosferatu and Sunrise pushed chiaroscuro lighting and moving camera toward pure mood. Its heavy shadow and menace later fed directly into the Hollywood horror film and film noir.
terms.example: The lopsided, hand-painted town of The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari — where streets lean and windows are shaped like wounds — shows set design itself standing in for a deranged mind.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; Lotte Eisner, The Haunted Screen; British Film Institute (BFI)

terms.short: The Florentine painter who broke from Byzantine flatness toward weight, space, and human emotion.
terms.definition: Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337) is traditionally credited with reorienting Western painting from the abstracted Byzantine manner toward naturalism, giving his figures solid, weighty bodies, believable settings, and convincing human feeling. He modeled forms with light and shadow, suggested three-dimensional space through simple architectural framing, and staged narratives with restrained, legible gesture and genuine pathos. Working chiefly in fresco, he was celebrated in his own time and held up by later writers as the founder of the modern, lifelike tradition. His achievement is called "proto-Renaissance" because it anticipated the systematic naturalism and perspective of the 15th century. Vasari later cast him as the artist who revived painting after the medieval centuries.
terms.example: Giotto's fresco cycle in the Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel, Padua (c. 1305), including the grieving angels and huddled mourners of the Lamentation, gives sacred drama unprecedented spatial depth and raw human emotion.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; Vasari, Lives of the Artists

terms.short: The painted decoration of hand-written books in the Gothic age, where much medieval painting survives.
terms.definition: Manuscript illumination decorated the pages of liturgical and devotional books — psalters, books of hours, bibles — with miniatures, historiated initials, gold leaf, and marginalia, executed in tempera and burnished gold on parchment. In the Gothic period (roughly 13th–15th centuries) illumination grew more naturalistic and narrative, with softer modeling, observed detail, and the elegant elongated figures of the "International Gothic." Workshops in Paris and the courts of Burgundy and France produced luxury commissions for aristocratic patrons. Because panel painting and fresco survive unevenly from the period, illuminated manuscripts are a crucial record of medieval pictorial invention. The Limbourg brothers brought the form to a peak of refinement.
terms.example: The Limbourg brothers' Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry (c. 1412–1416), with its calendar pages of seasonal labor and aristocratic leisure beneath jewel-like skies, marks the height of International Gothic illumination.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; C. de Hamel, A History of Illuminated Manuscripts

terms.short: The Greek effort to explain music as ratio and mode laid the theoretical foundation of the Western tradition.
terms.definition: Ancient Greek thinkers treated music as a branch of mathematics, with Pythagoras and his followers deriving consonant intervals (octave, fifth, fourth) from simple whole-number string-length ratios. Theorists such as Aristoxenus organized melody into tonoi or modes, each defined by a characteristic arrangement of intervals, and ethos doctrine held that different modes shaped character and emotion. Almost no Greek music survives in sound, but its theory was transmitted through Boethius into the Middle Ages, where the mode names were reassigned to the church modes. Pythagorean tuning, built from stacked pure fifths, governed Western pitch thinking for centuries.
terms.example: The Seikilos epitaph, a short song carved on a tombstone (c. 1st century CE) with both lyrics and notation, is the oldest complete piece of music that survives and shows the Greek diatonic scale in practice.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 1; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Greek music'

terms.short: The Athenian dramatic form perfected by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides.
terms.definition: Greek tragedy arose in 5th-century BCE Athens from choral performances honoring Dionysus and matured into a drama of moral conflict, fate, and suffering. Aeschylus expanded the cast to allow genuine dialogue and wrote the Oresteia; Sophocles added a third actor and composed Oedipus Rex and Antigone; Euripides brought psychological realism and skepticism to plays like Medea. Performed at civic festivals, tragedies combined spoken episodes with sung choral odes. Aristotle's Poetics later codified their structure, including catharsis and the tragic reversal (peripeteia).
terms.example: In Sophocles's Oedipus Rex, the king's investigation into a plague unknowingly uncovers his own guilt — the archetypal tragic reversal in which the search for truth destroys the seeker.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to Classical Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The painted pottery of ancient Greece, the principal surviving record of Greek pictorial art.
terms.definition: Greek vase painting decorated ceramic vessels with mythological and everyday scenes, evolving from geometric ornament through the black-figure technique — figures painted in slip silhouette and detailed by incision against the red clay — to the red-figure technique pioneered in Athens around 530 BCE, which reversed the scheme so figures were left in reserved red clay against a black ground, allowing brushed interior detail and greater anatomical naturalism. Painters such as Exekias (black-figure) and the Berlin Painter and Euphronios (red-figure) signed and individualized their work. The vessels' shapes encoded function — amphorae, kraters, kylixes — and their imagery is a primary source for Greek myth, ritual, and daily life. The medium fixed conventions of contour drawing and narrative composition that underlie later Western image-making.
terms.example: Exekias's amphora showing Achilles and Ajax absorbed in a board game (c. 540–530 BCE) crystallizes black-figure at its height — taut silhouettes, fine incised detail, and a charged moment of stillness before battle.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; J. Boardman, Athenian Black Figure / Red Figure Vases

terms.short: The unaccompanied monophonic liturgical chant of the Western church and the cradle of music notation.
terms.definition: Gregorian chant is a body of monophonic, unaccompanied sacred song sung in Latin for the Roman Catholic liturgy, traditionally associated by legend with Pope Gregory I. Its free, text-driven rhythm and modal melodies were transmitted orally for centuries before being written down. Beginning around the 9th century, neumes were added above the text to indicate melodic shape, evolving into staff notation credited to Guido of Arezzo, who also developed solmization syllables for sight-singing. This standardization of pitch on the staff was the decisive technical step that made later polyphony and the whole written Western tradition possible.
terms.example: A chant such as the Easter introit 'Resurrexi' shows the style: a single modal line, no harmony, with the melody expanding into long melismas on important words of the text.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 1; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Gregorian chant'

terms.short: The foundational Greek oral epics attributed to Homer that open the Western literary tradition.
terms.definition: The Iliad and the Odyssey, traditionally attributed to Homer (c. 8th century BCE), are long narrative poems in dactylic hexameter that emerged from a centuries-old oral tradition. The Iliad treats the rage of Achilles during the Trojan War; the Odyssey follows Odysseus's homecoming. Their formulaic epithets and repeated phrases reflect the techniques of bardic improvisation later analyzed by Milman Parry and Albert Lord. As the earliest surviving works of Western literature, they set the conventions of epic — the invocation of the Muse, in medias res openings, and the heroic code.
terms.example: The Iliad begins by naming the wrath of Achilles, then narrows from the whole Trojan War to a single quarrel with Agamemnon — a compression that became the model for epic focus.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Classical Dictionary; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The movement that took painting outdoors to capture fleeting light, color, and the passing moment.
terms.definition: Impressionism, named mockingly after Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872), arose in 1870s France as painters worked outdoors (en plein air) to record the changing effects of light, weather, and atmosphere with rapid, broken brushstrokes and bright, unmixed color. Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Camille Pissarro, Edgar Degas, and Berthe Morisot exhibited independently from 1874, rejecting the academic Salon's smooth finish and historical subjects for scenes of modern leisure, city life, and landscape. They emphasized optical sensation over outline and detail, letting the eye blend dabs of color. New portable paint tubes and the railway made plein-air work practical. The movement decisively opened the modern era of painting.
terms.example: Monet's series of the Rouen Cathedral facade, painted repeatedly under different light, treats the same stone front as a shifting field of colored light rather than a fixed object.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: A turn-of-the-century French style prizing timbre, color, and atmosphere over traditional development.
terms.definition: Impressionist music, associated above all with Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel, loosened functional tonality in favor of evocative color, fluid form, and the sheer sensuous quality of sound. Composers drew on whole-tone and pentatonic scales, modal and parallel chords, and shimmering orchestration to suggest mood and image rather than to argue a thematic narrative. The label borrows from painting, though Debussy disliked it, and the music shares with Symbolist poetry an interest in suggestion over statement. This emphasis on timbre as a primary element profoundly shaped 20th-century music.
terms.example: Debussy's orchestral Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894), inspired by a Mallarmé poem, opens with a famously sinuous flute solo and floating harmony that many historians treat as the threshold of musical modernism.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 4; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Claude Debussy'

terms.short: A post-WWII Italian movement that filmed ordinary lives on real streets with non-professional actors and minimal artifice.
terms.definition: Born in the rubble of fascist Italy, neorealism turned away from studio polish toward the everyday struggles of the poor and working class. Directors shot on location with available light, cast non-professional actors, and built loose, episodic stories from contemporary social reality. Roberto Rossellini's Rome, Open City and Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves typified an ethics of attention to ordinary suffering. Though short-lived, the movement reset international cinema's sense of what film could honestly depict and seeded later realist and new-wave movements across the world.
terms.example: In De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948), a working man and his son search the streets of Rome for a stolen bicycle — played by non-actors amid real crowds — making an undramatic search carry the weight of a whole class's precarity.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; André Bazin, What Is Cinema?; The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: The American art form built on blues roots, syncopation, and improvisation that reshaped 20th-century music worldwide.
terms.definition: Jazz emerged in early-20th-century New Orleans from the convergence of the blues, ragtime syncopation, brass-band traditions, and African American musical practice, centered on improvisation over a steady harmonic framework. It evolved rapidly through distinct styles: the soloist-driven hot jazz of the 1920s, the danceable big-band swing of the 1930s, and the fast, harmonically intricate bebop of the 1940s that reclaimed jazz as a listener's art. Improvisation, swing feel, and a flexible approach to pitch and timbre give the music its identity. Jazz spread globally and fed back into concert music, film, and popular song.
terms.example: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings (1925–28) demonstrated the power of the individual improvising soloist, while Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie's bebop a generation later redefined the music's harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Ted Gioia, The History of Jazz; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'jazz'

terms.short: American vernacular dance with African-American roots — rhythmic, syncopated jazz dance and the percussive footwork of tap.
terms.definition: Jazz and tap dance grew out of African-American vernacular movement, blending West African rhythmic traditions with European step forms in the social and theatrical life of the United States. Tap dance crystallized the body as a percussion instrument, with metal-plated shoes articulating intricate rhythms; the Harlem Renaissance and later figures such as Bill Bojangles Robinson and the virtuosic Nicholas Brothers brought it to stage and screen. Jazz dance, syncopated and grounded, spread through the swing era's social dances such as the Lindy Hop at venues like the Savoy Ballroom and into Broadway and Hollywood. Choreographers including Katherine Dunham, Jack Cole, and later Bob Fosse shaped jazz dance into a theatrical idiom. These forms anchored popular and commercial dance and fed directly into later street styles.
terms.example: The Nicholas Brothers' flying split-and-staircase number in the film Stormy Weather (1943) showcased tap dance at its athletic and rhythmic peak, an emblem of the African-American vernacular tradition.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The German master whose contrapuntal and harmonic command marks the summit of the Baroque.
terms.definition: Johann Sebastian Bach synthesized the national styles and genres of his age into a body of work of unmatched contrapuntal density and harmonic logic. Working as an organist, court musician, and finally cantor in Leipzig, he produced hundreds of sacred cantatas, the great Passions, organ and keyboard works, concertos, and exhaustive demonstrations of compositional craft. His writing perfected fugue and explored the full implications of functional tonality, including equal-temperament tuning that allowed music in every key. Largely neglected as old-fashioned after his death, his music was revived in the 19th century and became foundational to Western pedagogy.
terms.example: The two books of The Well-Tempered Clavier present a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key, a comprehensive demonstration that a single tuning could serve all twenty-four keys.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Christoph Wolff, Johann Sebastian Bach: The Learned Musician; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Johann Sebastian Bach'

terms.short: The archetypal Renaissance master whose sfumato dissolved hard outlines into atmospheric softness.
terms.definition: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) fused empirical observation with painterly innovation, most distinctively through sfumato — the imperceptible blending of tones "like smoke" that softens contours and models form with subtle gradations of light and shade. He grounded his art in studies of anatomy, optics, botany, and atmospheric perspective, by which distant forms grow hazier and bluer. His handful of finished paintings show psychological depth, pyramidal compositions, and an unprecedented unity of figure and air. Working in oil, he layered translucent glazes to achieve luminous, almost dimensionless transitions. He embodied the ideal of the artist as scientist and theorist as much as craftsman.
terms.example: The Mona Lisa (c. 1503–1519) demonstrates sfumato in the unfixed corners of the mouth and eyes and the dissolving, vaporous landscape behind her, producing the sitter's famously elusive expression.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; M. Kemp, Leonardo da Vinci

terms.short: The geometric system that let painters construct convincing pictorial depth on a flat surface.
terms.definition: Linear (one-point) perspective is a method of representing three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional plane by converging parallel lines toward a single vanishing point on the horizon, with objects diminishing systematically with distance. It was demonstrated by the architect Filippo Brunelleschi in Florence around 1413–1420 and codified by Leon Battista Alberti in his treatise On Painting (1435), which framed the picture as a "window" onto a measured space. Masaccio applied it monumentally in painting, lending figures architectural solidity and rational placement. The system made the depicted world measurable and unified, anchoring it to a single fixed viewpoint. It became a defining tool of Renaissance illusionism and Western image-making for centuries.
terms.example: Masaccio's fresco of the Holy Trinity in Santa Maria Novella, Florence (c. 1427), constructs a coffered barrel-vaulted chapel receding to a single vanishing point, making the painted architecture appear to open into the wall.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Alberti, On Painting; Gombrich, The Story of Art; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: The composer who bridged Classical and Romantic, expanding form and turning music into personal expression.
terms.definition: Ludwig van Beethoven inherited the Classical style from Haydn and Mozart and transformed it, stretching forms to unprecedented length and intensity and charging music with autobiographical struggle. He expanded the symphony, added voices and choral forces to it, and pushed sonata form, harmony, and the piano to new dramatic extremes. Composing much of his greatest work while progressively deaf, he made personal heroism and triumph-over-adversity a central theme, reshaping the public image of the composer as an autonomous artist. His late quartets and sonatas opened paths that Romantic composers would follow for the rest of the century.
terms.example: The Symphony No. 9 (1824) closes with a choral setting of Schiller's 'Ode to Joy', the first time voices entered a symphony in this way, redefining the scale and ambition of the genre.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven: The Music and the Life; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Ludwig van Beethoven'

terms.short: Fiction in which the marvelous is narrated matter-of-factly alongside the everyday.
terms.definition: Magical realism presents fantastic or supernatural events as ordinary, woven seamlessly into a realistic narrative without surprise. Rooted in earlier currents and in Jorge Luis Borges's metaphysical fictions, it became the signature mode of the Latin American 'Boom' of the 1960s. Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude epitomizes it, chronicling generations of the Buendía family in Macondo where ascensions to heaven and decades of rain are reported as plainly as the weather. The mode let writers fuse myth, history, and politics, and it spread worldwide through authors such as Isabel Allende and Salman Rushdie.
terms.example: In One Hundred Years of Solitude, a character ascends bodily into the sky while folding laundry, and the villagers' chief concern is the loss of the sheets — the marvelous reported with the flat tone of a household event.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to Spanish Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The era when cutting and tailoring emerged and dress became legally regulated by rank.
terms.definition: Across the Middle Ages dress shifted from loose draped tunics toward fitted, sewn garments as cutting techniques (curved seams, set-in sleeves, lacing, and buttons) developed in the 14th century. The close-fitting cotehardie and the voluminous, often dagged houppelande gave silhouettes that genuinely followed or exaggerated the body for the first time. Sumptuary laws attempted to fix who could wear which furs, fabrics, and colors, treating clothing as a legible map of social order. Dress thus became a site of regulation and aspiration, with rising merchants pressing against the limits set for them.
terms.example: The 14th-century cotehardie, laced tight to the torso with rows of small buttons, marks the moment tailoring let clothing trace the body — and prompted sumptuary statutes policing such display.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: Medieval communal and court dancing — the sung circle-dance carole, instrumental estampie, and the imagery of the danse macabre.
terms.definition: Through the European Middle Ages dance lived as folk and court practice rather than a notated theatrical tradition, much of it documented only indirectly. The carole, a sung chain or circle dance, was widespread, while the estampie survives as one of the earliest named instrumental dance forms. The Church regarded much popular dancing with suspicion even as dance flourished at courts and feasts. The danse macabre, the Dance of Death, became a powerful late-medieval allegory in art and verse, picturing skeletons leading people of every rank in a leveling procession. These traditions seeded the social-dance repertoire that Renaissance dancing masters would later codify.
terms.example: Surviving manuscripts preserve estampies as some of the oldest written-down instrumental dances, while the danse macabre appeared painted on charnel-house and church walls such as the celebrated cycle once at the Cemetery of the Innocents in Paris.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The medieval invention of multiple simultaneous voices, from early organum to the rhythmic sophistication of ars nova.
terms.definition: Medieval polyphony grew from organum, in which a second voice was added to a chant, into the elaborate compositions of the Notre-Dame school in 12th- and 13th-century Paris, where Léonin and Pérotin layered florid upper voices over sustained chant tenors. This period developed rhythmic modes and, crucially, mensural notation that could specify durations precisely. In the 14th century the ars nova, theorized by Philippe de Vitry and realized by Guillaume de Machaut, expanded rhythmic and harmonic resources, including isorhythm. Machaut, also a major poet, composed the first polyphonic setting of the Mass Ordinary by a single named author.
terms.example: Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame (c. 1360s) is a landmark: a four-voice polyphonic Mass conceived as a unified cyclic work by one composer rather than an anonymous assembly of chants.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 1; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'ars nova'

terms.short: The chivalric and Arthurian narratives of knighthood, quest, and courtly love.
terms.definition: Medieval romance flourished from the 12th century as a vernacular narrative of knightly adventure, replacing the martial epic's collective glory with individual quest and refined emotion. Chrétien de Troyes shaped the Arthurian tradition with romances of Lancelot, Perceval, and the Grail, while the ideology of courtly love (fin'amor) governed the knight's devotion to an idealized lady. The matter of Britain, France, and Rome supplied recurring story cycles, culminating in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Malory's later Le Morte d'Arthur. The form prized marvels, allegory, and a code of honor.
terms.example: In Chrétien's Lancelot, the knight hesitates a single step before climbing into a cart to rescue Guinevere — and that flicker of shame at lost dignity dramatizes the whole tension between honor and love.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The intellectual wit of the Metaphysical poets and Milton's biblical epic in English.
terms.definition: Seventeenth-century English poetry took two great Baroque directions. The Metaphysical poets — chiefly John Donne, with George Herbert and Andrew Marvell — fused passionate argument with startling 'conceits,' extended intellectual metaphors yoking unlike ideas, in compact, rhetorically intense lyrics. John Milton, working in the same century but on an epic scale, composed Paradise Lost (1667), a blank-verse retelling of the Fall that aimed to 'justify the ways of God to men' and gave Satan a magnificent, ambiguous grandeur. Together they mark the Baroque era's appetite for elaborate design, paradox, and dramatic intensity.
terms.example: Donne's 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning' compares two parting lovers to the legs of a drawing compass — one fixed, one roaming — an audacious conceit that makes geometry an emblem of constancy.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of English Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The sculptor-painter whose Sistine ceiling set the standard for monumental High Renaissance figuration.
terms.definition: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564), primarily a sculptor, painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome between 1508 and 1512 at the commission of Pope Julius II, covering it with scenes from Genesis framed by an illusionistic architecture of nudes (ignudi), prophets, and sibyls. His figures are sculpturally muscular and dynamic, conceived as bodies in heroic motion, expressing the period's confidence in the human form as the vehicle of the divine. He later painted the Last Judgment on the chapel's altar wall (1536–1541), a turbulent, twisting mass of bodies that helped shape Mannerism. His command of anatomy, foreshortening, and grandeur defined the High Renaissance terribilità. The ceiling remains one of the most influential achievements in Western painting.
terms.example: The Creation of Adam on the Sistine ceiling — the near-touching fingers of God and Adam across a charged gap — distills Michelangelo's fusion of physical power and spiritual reach.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; Vasari, Lives of the Artists

terms.short: The early-twentieth-century revolt against ballet's formality, inventing a new expressive vocabulary rooted in the dancer's own body and feeling.
terms.definition: Modern dance arose as a deliberate rejection of ballet's codified technique, pointe shoes, and aristocratic conventions in favor of barefoot, expressive movement. Isadora Duncan, dancing freely in flowing tunics and drawing on Greek and natural imagery, became its pioneering prophet in the 1900s. In the United States the form matured through Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn's Denishawn school, and then through Martha Graham, whose contraction-and-release technique and dramatic works such as Appalachian Spring (1944) built a rigorous new grammar. Doris Humphrey and, in Germany, the Ausdruckstanz of Mary Wigman pursued parallel expressionist paths. Modern dance established that serious theatrical dance need not be ballet, opening the door to continual reinvention.
terms.example: Martha Graham's Appalachian Spring (1944), set to Aaron Copland's score, used her percussive contraction-and-release technique to dramatize an American frontier wedding, exemplifying modern dance's invented expressive vocabulary.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: ~1860–1945: the break with tradition — abstraction, atonality, stream of consciousness, and the birth of cinema.
terms.definition: Modernism is the deliberate rupture with inherited conventions in the face of industrial, urban, and scientific upheaval. Painting moved from Impressionism's broken light to the fractured space of Cubism and the dream-logic of Surrealism; music broke tonality (Schoenberg, Stravinsky) and birthed jazz; literature pursued symbolism, stream of consciousness, and the fragmented modernist poem; ballet was revolutionised by the Ballets Russes and overturned by modern dance; fashion was liberated by Chanel; and an entirely new art — film — was invented and rapidly matured. 'Make it new' is the era's command.
terms.example: 1913 alone saw Stravinsky's riot-provoking 'Rite of Spring' (danced by the Ballets Russes), the Armory Show carrying Cubism to America, and Proust's first volume — three forms breaking with the past in the same season.
terms.source: Gombrich, The Story of Art (Modernism); Bordwell & Thompson, Film History (early cinema); Encyclopædia Britannica (Modernism)

terms.short: The fragmentary, allusive verse of Eliot and Pound that remade poetry after 1900.
terms.definition: Modernist poetry, led by T. S. Eliot and Ezra Pound, broke with Romantic and Victorian convention in favor of fragmentation, allusion, and 'making it new.' Pound's Imagism demanded hard, precise images and the discarding of ornament, while his later Cantos pursued a sprawling collage of history and quotation. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) assembled a fractured, multilingual mosaic of cultural ruin that became the era's defining poem, abetted by Pound's editing. The movement favored free verse, juxtaposition, and impersonality, demanding an active, interpreting reader.
terms.example: Eliot's The Waste Land splices a London commuter crowd, a Buddhist sermon, and lines in several languages without transitions — a deliberately broken surface that mirrors the post-war sense of a shattered civilization.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of Poetry; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The high-waisted, columnar white muslin gown inspired by antique drapery.
terms.definition: Around 1800 women's dress abandoned stiff hoops and heavy structure for a slender, high-waisted line that fell straight from beneath the bust, echoing the draped statuary of Greece and Rome. Lightweight white cotton muslin became the fashionable fabric, prized for its classical simplicity and (controversially) its near-transparency. This Empire or Regency style coincided with Neoclassicism in painting and architecture, expressing Enlightenment ideals of natural form and republican restraint. It was a sharp reaction against Rococo excess, and one of the few moments when fashion abandoned the corseted, structured body almost entirely.
terms.example: The Regency white muslin gown — waist just under the bust, skirt falling in a straight column — translated antique drapery into modern dress and briefly freed women from rigid stays.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: The austere revival of classical order and moral seriousness led by Jacques-Louis David.
terms.definition: Neoclassicism arose in the later eighteenth century as a deliberate return to the clarity, restraint, and ethical gravity of Greek and Roman antiquity, spurred by Enlightenment ideals and the excavations of Pompeii and Herculaneum. In painting it favored firm drawing (line over color), sculptural figures, sober palettes, shallow stage-like space, and subjects of civic virtue, sacrifice, and stoic duty. Jacques-Louis David became its leading figure and the visual voice of the French Revolution, channeling Roman exempla into contemporary political message. The style rejected Rococo frivolity for moral and formal discipline. It dominated official European art around 1800 and shaped academic painting thereafter.
terms.example: David's Oath of the Horatii (1784) lines up three brothers swearing on raised swords to die for Rome — rigid, friezelike, lit with cold clarity — making personal sacrifice for the state a stark civic ideal.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: The late-1960s–1970s American renaissance in which a generation of director-driven filmmakers revitalized Hollywood with personal, formally daring films.
terms.definition: As the old studio system collapsed and the production code gave way to a ratings system, a film-school-educated generation steeped in European art cinema took the reins. Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, Robert Altman, and their peers made morally complex, stylistically adventurous films aimed at adults — works like The Godfather, Taxi Driver, and Nashville. They imported the auteur ideal and New Wave techniques into the American mainstream, foregrounding antiheroes, ambiguity, and director control. The era's creative freedom narrowed once the blockbuster reordered the industry's economics.
terms.example: Coppola's The Godfather (1972) — operatic, slow-burning, and uncompromisingly the director's vision — shows New Hollywood turning a genre crime story into a personal American tragedy with full studio resources.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; Peter Biskind, Easy Riders, Raging Bulls; British Film Institute (BFI)

terms.short: The movement that embraced advertising, comics, and mass-produced imagery as the stuff of art.
terms.definition: Pop Art emerged in Britain and the United States in the 1950s and 1960s as a reaction against the introspective seriousness of Abstract Expressionism, turning instead to the imagery of consumer culture — advertising, packaging, comic strips, celebrity, and mass media. Andy Warhol used silkscreen to reproduce soup cans, Marilyn Monroe, and Campbell's branding with deadpan, machine-like repetition that blurred fine art and commodity, while Roy Lichtenstein enlarged comic-book panels complete with Ben-Day dots and speech balloons. The movement adopted commercial techniques and a cool, ironic detachment, questioning originality, authorship, and the boundary between high and low culture. It reflected and critiqued postwar abundance and media saturation. Pop opened directly onto postmodern and contemporary art.
terms.example: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans (1962), thirty-two near-identical canvases each depicting a single soup variety, elevates supermarket packaging to gallery art and flattens the distinction between artwork and product.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: The diverse generation after Impressionism that pushed color and form toward personal expression and structure.
terms.definition: Post-Impressionism is a retrospective label for the varied French painting of roughly 1885–1905 that built on Impressionism's color while rejecting its fleeting surface for greater structure, symbolism, and emotional or expressive intensity. Vincent van Gogh charged thick, swirling brushwork with personal feeling; Paul Cézanne sought the underlying geometry of nature, analyzing form into planes that would lead toward Cubism; Georges Seurat applied Pointillist dots with quasi-scientific rigor; and Paul Gauguin used flat, symbolic color and "primitivist" subjects. There was no single style but a shared move beyond optical impression toward the artist's conception. These innovations became the seedbed of twentieth-century modernism. Each path opened a distinct door to abstraction.
terms.example: Van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889) turns a night sky into churning spirals of luminous blue and yellow, paint applied in vehement strokes that express inner turbulence rather than literal observation.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: 1945–present: pluralism, pastiche, mass media, and the dissolving line between high and popular art.
terms.definition: After 1945 a single dominant style gives way to plurality, irony, appropriation, and the collapse of the high/low divide. Abstract Expressionism and then Pop Art remade painting; popular music (rock, pop, hip-hop) became the era's dominant sound; magical realism and postmodern fiction reshaped the novel; postmodern, contemporary, and street dance broke ballet's monopoly; Dior's New Look, the 1960s youthquake, and global ready-to-wear democratised fashion; and cinema moved through neorealism, the new waves, New Hollywood, the blockbuster, world cinema, and the digital/streaming age. Media saturation and global exchange define the present.
terms.example: Warhol's silkscreens of soup cans and celebrities collapse the high/low boundary the way sampling does in hip-hop and pastiche does in postmodern fiction — one cross-art logic of quotation running through painting, music, and literature at once.
terms.source: Janson's History of Art (Postwar & Contemporary); Bordwell & Thompson, Film History (postwar cinema); Encyclopædia Britannica (Postmodernism)

terms.short: The mid-century avant-garde that stripped dance of narrative and hierarchy, embracing chance, everyday movement, and pure form.
terms.definition: Postmodern dance challenged even modern dance's expressive and dramatic premises, questioning what could count as dance at all. Merce Cunningham separated dance from music and narrative, using chance procedures — including the I Ching and later computers — to determine movement and treating space without a fixed front, often in collaboration with composer John Cage. In the 1960s the Judson Dance Theater in New York, with artists such as Yvonne Rainer, Steve Paxton, and Trisha Brown, embraced pedestrian movement, task-based structures, and a refusal of virtuosic spectacle, captured in Rainer's polemical No Manifesto. Paxton's contact improvisation introduced a new partnering practice based on shared weight and momentum. This radical openness redefined dance as conceptual inquiry and dissolved the boundary between art and ordinary motion.
terms.example: At the Judson Memorial Church in the early 1960s, Yvonne Rainer's Trio A presented continuous, unaccented, task-like movement that deliberately refused spectacle, epitomizing postmodern dance's rejection of theatrical display.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The self-conscious, playful fiction that foregrounds its own artifice and questions narrative truth.
terms.definition: Postmodern fiction, emerging after World War II, treats the novel as a self-aware construct, embracing metafiction, fragmentation, irony, and the blurring of high and popular culture. Jorge Luis Borges's labyrinthine stories of infinite libraries and forking paths supplied its philosophical seeds; Thomas Pynchon's encyclopedic Gravity's Rainbow heaped paranoia, history, and entropy into dense systems; Italo Calvino played overtly with form in If on a winter's night a traveler, a novel about reading a novel. These writers distrust grand narratives and stable meaning, often turning the act of storytelling itself into the subject.
terms.example: Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveler addresses 'you, the reader' and keeps interrupting itself with the openings of ten different novels — a book that is largely about the impossibility and pleasure of finishing one.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The rise of designer ready-made clothing and the global, seasonal fashion system.
terms.definition: Ready-to-wear (prêt-à-porter) is standardized-size clothing made for sale off the rack rather than fitted to one client, and from the 1960s onward couturiers and new designers embraced it as the industry's commercial core. Designer labels licensed their names and built brands spanning clothing, accessories, perfume, and advertising, turning fashion into a global business of seasonal collections, runway shows, and trade fairs. The structure separated prestige-setting couture from mass-market profit while binding both to a calendar of fashion weeks in Paris, Milan, New York, and London. Ready-to-wear democratized designer style and made fashion a worldwide industrial system.
terms.example: Yves Saint Laurent's 1966 Rive Gauche boutique line gave a major couturier's name to ready-made clothing, signaling that designer prestige and off-the-rack scale would now drive the fashion system together.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("haute couture" / "ready-to-wear")

terms.short: The mid-nineteenth-century insistence on depicting ordinary modern life without idealization.
terms.definition: Realism emerged in France around 1850 as a rejection of both Neoclassical idealism and Romantic fantasy, insisting that art depict the contemporary world — peasants, laborers, and unglamorous modern life — honestly and on a serious scale. Gustave Courbet was its combative champion, painting common subjects with the monumental ambition once reserved for history painting and provoking the establishment by refusing to flatter. Realists addressed social conditions and the dignity (and hardship) of ordinary people, often with a political edge tied to the upheavals of 1848. The movement valued direct observation over convention and academic polish. It set the stage for the modernist break by relocating art's subject to the here and now.
terms.example: Courbet's A Burial at Ornans (1849–1850) depicts a provincial funeral on a vast canvas usually reserved for grand history, crowding ordinary villagers into a scene that scandalized critics by its plainness and scale.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: The supreme painter of the Dutch Golden Age, master of light, shadow, and inward character.
terms.definition: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669) worked in the prosperous, largely Protestant Dutch Republic, whose open art market favored portraits, group portraits, genre scenes, and landscapes over religious commissions. He absorbed Caravaggesque chiaroscuro and made light an instrument of psychological revelation, using warm tonal depth, thick impasto, and an etcher's economy to convey age, thought, and feeling. His unsparing series of self-portraits charts a life across decades, while his history paintings stage drama through gesture and selective illumination. He stands within a broader flourishing that included Frans Hals, Jan Steen, and the landscapists. His handling of paint and emotional depth made him a touchstone for later generations.
terms.example: The Night Watch (1642), Rembrandt's huge militia group portrait, breaks the static convention by setting the company in mid-stride under dramatic, uneven light, turning a corporate commission into a scene of movement and theater.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; S. Schama, Rembrandt's Eyes

terms.short: Italian Renaissance court dance, codified by professional dancing masters whose treatises gave Europe its first detailed choreographic record.
terms.definition: In fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian and French courts, dance became a refined art of deportment and a marker of noble grace, taught by professional dancing masters. Domenico da Piacenza and his pupils Antonio Cornazano and Guglielmo Ebreo wrote the earliest surviving European dance treatises, theorizing qualities such as measure, memory, and the carriage of the body. Later in the sixteenth century Fabritio Caroso (Il Ballarino, Nobiltà di dame) and Cesare Negri set out detailed steps and floor patterns for the balletto and other court dances. These books transmitted a repertoire of paired social dances and gave choreography a written vocabulary. The Renaissance court dance is the direct ancestor of the spectacular ballet de cour that would crystallize in France.
terms.example: Fabritio Caroso's Nobiltà di dame (1600) laid out named balletti step by step for aristocratic dancers, the kind of codified court spectacle that fed into Catherine de' Medici's lavish festival the Ballet comique de la reine (1581).
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: Structured, ornament-laden court dress that made wealth and status conspicuously visible.
terms.definition: Renaissance dress turned the body into an architectural display of rank, using stiffened bodices, padding, and rigid understructures to impose a fashionable shape. Decorative techniques such as slashing (slits cut to reveal contrasting linings) and elaborate embroidery advertised the cost of cloth and labor, while the starched ruff grew into an extravagant frame around the face. Spanish, Italian, French, and English courts each set styles, and rich silks, velvets, and imported dyes signaled access to global trade. Dress became a deliberate instrument of magnificence and political image-making for monarchs and nobles.
