terms.example: The towering starched ruff of the Elizabethan court — wired, pleated, and impractical — crystallized dress as pure status display, demanding servants, time, and money simply to wear.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: The recovery of classical learning that reoriented literature toward human experience.
terms.definition: Renaissance humanism, beginning in 14th-century Italy, revived the study of classical Greek and Latin texts and placed human dignity, eloquence, and individual experience at the center of letters. Petrarch, often called its father, refined the sonnet in his Canzoniere and modeled a new self-aware lyric subjectivity. The movement spread across Europe through scholars such as Erasmus, while in France Michel de Montaigne invented the essay (essais, 'attempts') as a flexible form of skeptical, first-person inquiry. Humanism supplied the intellectual ground from which Renaissance drama and the modern novel grew.
terms.example: Montaigne's essays circle questions like 'On Cannibals' by reasoning from his own doubts and digressions rather than from authority — founding a genre defined by a thinking mind watching itself.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The golden age of imitative vocal counterpoint, perfected by Josquin and codified by Palestrina.
terms.definition: Renaissance polyphony refined the interweaving of independent vocal lines into smooth, balanced counterpoint governed by careful control of consonance and dissonance. Franco-Flemish composers led by Josquin des Prez made pervasive imitation, where each voice enters with the same motive, the central organizing principle, achieving a new expressive union of words and music. Later in the 16th century Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina produced a model of clear, serene sacred counterpoint that the Counter-Reformation church embraced and that theorists for centuries taught as the standard of pure style. Madrigals and the rise of music printing spread these techniques across Europe.
terms.example: Palestrina's Missa Papae Marcelli (published 1567) became the textbook example of polyphony in which the words remain audible, later mythologized as the Mass that saved sacred polyphony from being banned.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 1; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Palestrina'

terms.short: Wagner reconceived opera as total artwork bound by leitmotifs and a continuously evolving harmonic flow.
terms.definition: Richard Wagner sought to fuse music, poetry, drama, and staging into a unified Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art, replacing the old number-opera of separate arias with continuous musical flow. He organized his vast dramas through leitmotifs, recurring musical themes attached to characters, objects, and ideas that develop as the drama unfolds. His chromatic harmony stretched tonality to its limits, a crisis point that would help open the door to atonality. Wagner built his own festival theater at Bayreuth to stage his works under controlled conditions.
terms.example: The four-opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen, premiered complete in 1876, spans roughly fifteen hours and weaves dozens of leitmotifs into an unprecedented mythological epic; its 'Tristan chord' in the related Tristan und Isolde became a symbol of harmonic ambiguity.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Barry Millington, The Wagner Compendium; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Richard Wagner'

terms.short: The recorded popular era, in which rock, pop, and hip-hop became the dominant music of the late 20th and early 21st centuries.
terms.definition: Rock and roll emerged in 1950s America from the fusion of blues, rhythm and blues, country, and gospel, carried by the new mass medium of the recording and amplified by the electric guitar. Over the following decades popular music fragmented and expanded into countless styles, with the recording studio itself becoming a compositional instrument and the album an artistic unit. From the 1970s onward hip-hop arose in the Bronx out of DJing, sampling, breakbeats, and rapped vocals, eventually becoming one of the most influential global genres. This era marks the shift of the cultural center of music from the concert hall and sheet music to recorded, broadcast, and now streamed sound.
terms.example: The Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) treated the studio as an instrument and the album as a unified work, while Grandmaster Flash and later artists turned turntables and sampling into the foundation of hip-hop.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Encyclopædia Britannica, 'rock' and 'hip-hop'; Jeff Chang, Can't Stop Won't Stop: A History of the Hip-Hop Generation

terms.short: The light, ornamental, pleasure-loving style of early-eighteenth-century France.
terms.definition: Rococo emerged in early-eighteenth-century France as a lighter, more intimate reaction to the grandeur of the Baroque, favoring delicate color, asymmetrical curving ornament, and themes of love, leisure, and aristocratic play. Antoine Watteau invented the fête galante — elegant figures dreaming or flirting in idyllic parkland — while later painters such as François Boucher and Jean-Honoré Fragonard pursued pastel sensuality, mythological eroticism, and decorative charm suited to private salons. The style mirrored the tastes of the French court and nobility before the Revolution. Its frivolity and luxury later drew moral criticism from Enlightenment and Neoclassical reformers. It nonetheless produced some of the most virtuoso and seductive painting of its age.
terms.example: Fragonard's The Swing (c. 1767) shows a young woman kicking off her slipper mid-arc while a hidden admirer gazes upward — a froth of pink silk, foliage, and flirtatious wit that epitomizes Rococo.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: Eighteenth-century court dress of wide panniers, pastel silks, and theatrical refinement.
terms.definition: Rococo women's dress widened the silhouette dramatically with panniers (side hoops) that extended the skirt outward, paired with the robe à la française and its loose Watteau back pleats. Surfaces were light, ornamental, and flirtatious — pastel silks, ruffles, bows, and floral trims that matched the period's painting. Marie Antoinette and her marchande de modes Rose Bertin made fashion a public obsession, with Bertin operating as an early celebrity tastemaker who dressed the queen and shaped trends. The extravagance of court dress also made clothing a flashpoint in the politics leading to the Revolution.
terms.example: Rose Bertin, dubbed the queen's "Minister of Fashion," supplied Marie Antoinette's elaborate panniered gowns and pouf hairstyles, an early model of the designer as celebrity and trendsetter.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: The wall painting and floor mosaic of the Roman world, preserved most vividly at Pompeii.
terms.definition: Roman fresco was applied to wet plaster (buon fresco) on the walls of villas and houses, surviving in quantity at Pompeii and Herculaneum after the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE sealed them. Scholars distinguish four Pompeian "styles," progressing from imitation masonry to elaborate architectural illusionism with deep, atmospheric perspective and mythological panels. Roman painters commanded shading, cast shadow, and an intuitive perspective that conveyed depth and volume centuries before its systematic codification. Alongside fresco, intricate tessellated mosaics — small cut stone or glass tesserae — decorated floors and walls with figural scenes, portraits, and pattern. Together they preserve the most complete picture we have of ancient illusionistic painting.
terms.example: The frescoes of the Villa of the Mysteries at Pompeii (c. 60–50 BCE) wrap a room in near life-size figures enacting a Dionysiac initiation against a vivid red ground, demonstrating Roman command of modeling, gesture, and continuous narrative.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; R. Ling, Roman Painting

terms.short: The golden-age Latin verse of Virgil and Ovid that reshaped the Greek inheritance for Rome.
terms.definition: Under Augustus, Latin poetry reached its classical height. Virgil's Aeneid (c. 19 BCE) recast Homeric epic as a national myth of Rome's founding through the wanderings of Aeneas, fusing the Iliad and Odyssey into a single political vision. Ovid's Metamorphoses gathered hundreds of transformation myths into a continuous mock-epic, becoming the great storehouse of classical mythology for later European art. Horace contributed the polished lyric ode and verse satire. These works transmitted Greek forms to the Latin West and, through them, to the entire medieval and Renaissance imagination.
terms.example: Ovid's Metamorphoses retells the myth of Daphne fleeing Apollo and turning into a laurel tree — a single image that supplied painters and poets with subject matter for two millennia.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Classical Dictionary; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The early-nineteenth-century ballet of ethereal sylphs and ghosts, dancing on pointe in white tulle, that made the ballerina the art's center.
terms.definition: Romantic ballet, flowering in Paris and beyond in the 1830s and 1840s, turned to the supernatural and the unattainable — sylphs, wilis, and spirits drawn from folklore and Romantic literature. Marie Taglioni's performance in her father Filippo Taglioni's La Sylphide (1832) epitomized the new ideal of weightless, otherworldly femininity and helped popularize dancing on the tips of the toes (en pointe). Giselle (1841), choreographed by Jean Coralli and Jules Perrot, became the defining masterwork, and its moonlit second act gave rise to the ballet blanc, a corps of women in long white tulle skirts. The era elevated the ballerina above the male dancer and fixed images that still define ballet in the popular imagination. Pointe work and the romantic tutu emerged as enduring technical and visual signatures.
terms.example: In Giselle (1841) the spectral Wilis of the second act move as a unified corps de ballet in white, the archetypal ballet blanc that crystallized Romantic ballet's vision of the supernatural feminine.
terms.source: The Oxford Dictionary of Dance; International Encyclopedia of Dance; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The early-nineteenth-century turn to emotion, the sublime, and the power of nature.
terms.definition: Romantic painting, flourishing in the first half of the nineteenth century, prized feeling, imagination, and individual experience over Neoclassical reason and rule, exalting the sublime grandeur of nature, exotic and historical drama, and the inner life. Eugène Delacroix led the French school with turbulent color, loose brushwork, and impassioned subjects; J. M. W. Turner in Britain dissolved storms, light, and sea into near-abstract atmosphere; and Caspar David Friedrich in Germany staged solitary figures before vast, spiritually charged landscapes. The movement responded to revolution, nationalism, and a new reverence for wild nature. It loosened academic finish in favor of expressive paint and mood. Its emphasis on subjectivity opened the way to later modern art.
terms.example: Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (c. 1818) places a lone man on a crag overlooking a fog-drowned landscape, an image of the individual confronting the sublime infinitude of nature.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: The early-19th-century poetry of feeling, nature, imagination, and the self.
terms.definition: Romantic poetry, flourishing from the 1790s, rejected Enlightenment restraint in favor of emotion, nature, imagination, and the individual sensibility. Wordsworth and Coleridge launched English Romanticism with Lyrical Ballads, championing ordinary speech and the spiritual power of nature, while Coleridge added the visionary and supernatural in 'Kubla Khan' and 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.' The second generation — Keats, Byron, and Shelley — pursued beauty, rebellion, and intensity, from Keats's sensuous odes to Byron's restless heroes and Shelley's revolutionary lyricism. The movement reframed the poet as a prophet of feeling and imagination.
terms.example: Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' meditates on figures frozen mid-gesture on an ancient vase, ending with the urn's cryptic equation of beauty and truth — a poem that makes a static art object a vehicle for longing.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of English Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: ~1800–1900: emotion, nature, the sublime, and the individual genius — plus Realism's counter-turn to ordinary life.
terms.definition: Romanticism elevated feeling, imagination, nature, and the sublime over Enlightenment restraint, exalting the individual artist as visionary. Delacroix and Turner charged painting with colour and atmosphere; Wordsworth, Keats, and the Romantic poets reinvented lyric; the symphony swelled (Berlioz, Brahms) and Wagner reimagined opera as total artwork; Romantic and then Imperial-Russian classical ballet flowered; and Victorian dress, then the birth of haute couture under Worth, formalised fashion. Mid-century Realism (Courbet, the realist novel) pushed back toward ordinary life, foreshadowing modernity.
terms.example: Wagner's idea of the Gesamtkunstwerk — uniting music, poetry, staging, and movement into one overwhelming whole — is Romanticism's cross-art ambition stated outright.
terms.source: Janson's History of Art (Romanticism & Realism); Taruskin, Oxford History of Western Music (Romantic era); Encyclopædia Britannica (Romanticism)

terms.short: The English playwright whose drama and verse define the height of the Elizabethan stage.
terms.definition: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote some thirty-seven plays and a sonnet sequence that mark the summit of English Renaissance literature. Working in the popular public theaters of Elizabethan and Jacobean London, he ranged across comedy, history, and tragedy, deepening characters through soliloquy and an unmatched command of blank verse. The great tragedies — Hamlet, King Lear, Macbeth, Othello — probe interiority, doubt, and moral collapse with a psychological density new to drama. His vast vocabulary and coinages shaped the English language itself, and his works became the central reference point of the Western dramatic canon.
terms.example: Hamlet pauses the entire revenge plot to weigh being against not-being in a soliloquy, turning a stage thriller into an inquiry into consciousness and dread.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of English Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: A 1920s Soviet movement that argued meaning in film is generated by the collision of edited shots, not by individual images.
terms.definition: Working in the early Soviet Union, filmmakers theorized that cinema's essence lay in editing — the juxtaposition of shots producing ideas no single shot contained. Lev Kuleshov's experiments demonstrated that audiences read emotion into a neutral face purely from the shot placed beside it (the 'Kuleshov effect'). Sergei Eisenstein developed a dialectical montage of conflict and rhythm for revolutionary ends, while Dziga Vertov pursued a documentary 'kino-eye' that reassembled raw life through cutting. The movement made editing the central creative act of film and shaped political and avant-garde cinema worldwide.
terms.example: The Odessa Steps sequence in Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin (1925) — a baby carriage tumbling down stone steps as soldiers fire — fragments the massacre into a rhythmic barrage of cuts that intensifies the horror far beyond what any continuous shot could.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; Sergei Eisenstein, Film Form; The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: Casual, subculture-rooted clothing that rose from the street to dominate contemporary fashion.
terms.definition: Streetwear is a contemporary mode built on casual garments — graphic T-shirts, hoodies, sneakers — that emerged from skate, surf, and hip-hop subcultures from the 1980s and 1990s. It inverted the old top-down model: style now bubbled up from youth communities, with brands like Stüssy and later Supreme using limited "drops," logos, and scarcity to build cult demand. By the 2010s luxury houses openly collaborated with streetwear labels and hired their designers, collapsing the line between high fashion and the street. Streetwear reflects a fashion system shaped by music, sport, identity, and social media rather than couture decree.
terms.example: Louis Vuitton's 2017 collaboration with the skate brand Supreme — and Virgil Abloh's 2018 appointment as its menswear director — marked streetwear's full ascent from subculture to the luxury runway.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("streetwear")

terms.short: The interwar movement that mined dreams and the unconscious for an art of the marvelous and uncanny.
terms.definition: Surrealism, launched in Paris in 1924 by the poet André Breton, sought to liberate the unconscious mind and reconcile dream with reality, drawing on Freudian psychoanalysis and the irrational. In painting it took two broad directions: the meticulous, illusionistic "dream" imagery of Salvador Dalí and René Magritte, who rendered impossible scenes with hallucinatory precision, and the automatist, biomorphic abstraction of Max Ernst, Joan Miró, and André Masson, who courted chance and the involuntary. Disorienting juxtapositions, metamorphosis, and the uncanny estrangement of ordinary objects were central. The movement extended into film, literature, and photography. Its imagery profoundly shaped later modern and popular visual culture.
terms.example: Dalí's The Persistence of Memory (1931), with its limp, melting watches draped over a barren dreamscape, became the emblematic image of Surrealism's pliable, dream-warped reality.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: The late-19th-century French poetry that prized suggestion, music, and the symbol over statement.
terms.definition: Symbolism arose in late-19th-century France as a reaction against realism and didactic verse, seeking to evoke states of mind through suggestion, musicality, and private symbols rather than direct description. Charles Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal, with its theory of correspondences linking the senses, is its great precursor; Stéphane Mallarmé pursued a difficult, allusive purity of language, and Arthur Rimbaud and Paul Verlaine pushed toward visionary disorder and pure sound. By detaching imagery from explanation, the Symbolists made the poem an autonomous object of mood and music — a decisive step toward modernist poetics.
terms.example: Rimbaud's 'Vowels' assigns a color to each vowel sound, treating language as synesthetic raw material rather than a transparent medium — an emblem of Symbolism's faith in the suggestive power of the word itself.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to French Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: ~1600–1750: drama, motion, and grandeur — chiaroscuro, tonality, the birth of opera, and court ballet.
terms.definition: The Baroque mobilised emotion and spectacle in service of Church, monarchy, and a rising merchant class. Painting deployed dramatic chiaroscuro (Caravaggio, Rembrandt) and intimate light (Vermeer); music established functional tonality and the basso continuo, gave birth to opera (Monteverdi), and culminated in Bach. The French court formalised ballet de cour under Louis XIV, and dress signalled absolute power. Theatricality — the staged, the dynamic, the overwhelming — is the period's through-line across every form.
terms.example: Monteverdi's early operas literally combine the arts of the era — poetry, staged spectacle, costume, dance interludes, and the new dramatic music — into one Baroque Gesamtkunstwerk avant la lettre.
terms.source: Janson's History of Art (Baroque); Taruskin, Oxford History of Western Music (tonality & opera); Encyclopædia Britannica (Baroque)

terms.short: The mid-19th-century invention of the named designer and the Paris fashion house.
terms.definition: Charles Frederick Worth, an Englishman working in Paris, transformed dressmaking from anonymous craft into authored design, founding the model of the haute couture house in the 1850s–60s. He presented seasonal collections on live mannequins, sewed his name into labels, and let clients choose from designs he originated rather than simply executing their instructions. This established the couturier as an artist-celebrity and Paris as the governing capital of high fashion, a position later formalized by the Chambre Syndicale. The system Worth created — designer authorship, the maison, the collection — underpins the modern fashion industry.
terms.example: Worth labeling his gowns and showing collections to clients like Empress Eugénie reframed the dressmaker as a creative authority, founding haute couture and the Paris-centered fashion house.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("Charles Frederick Worth")

terms.short: Opera emerged around 1600 from attempts to revive Greek drama through music, with Monteverdi giving it its first masterpiece.
terms.definition: Opera was born in Italy around 1600 when the Florentine Camerata, seeking to recover the emotional power of ancient Greek tragedy, championed monody and recitative, a sung speech driven by a single melodic line over continuo. Claudio Monteverdi transformed these experiments into expressive drama, drawing on both the older polyphonic style and the new monodic one to portray character and feeling. His use of orchestration, dissonance, and arioso writing made music a vehicle for psychological action. Opera quickly became a public spectacle, with the first commercial opera houses opening in Venice within decades.
terms.example: Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) is widely regarded as the first great opera, using a richly varied orchestra and the lament of Orpheus to fuse drama, poetry, and music.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 2; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'opera'

terms.short: The mid-1970s shift to wide-release, heavily marketed event films built for mass simultaneous audiences and franchises.
terms.definition: Steven Spielberg's Jaws (1975) and George Lucas's Star Wars (1977) inaugurated a new economic model: open a film on thousands of screens at once, back it with saturation television advertising, and chase the largest possible opening weekend. High-concept premises, spectacle, sequels, and merchandising became the industry's growth engine, displacing the director-driven freedoms of New Hollywood. The model favored special effects, recognizable franchises, and global appeal, reshaping which films got made and how. It remains the dominant commercial logic of studio cinema, intensified by later superhero franchises.
terms.example: Star Wars (1977) opened to lines around the block, spawned sequels, toys, and a merchandising empire — demonstrating how a single film could become a self-perpetuating franchise rather than a standalone work.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; Tom Shone, Blockbuster; British Film Institute (BFI)

terms.short: The mid-18th-century turn to clear melody, balanced phrasing, and the dramatic architecture of sonata form.
terms.definition: The Classical style that crystallized in Vienna around the later 18th century favored singing melody, transparent textures, and clear periodic phrasing over the dense counterpoint of the Baroque. Its central principle was sonata form, a dramatic plan of exposition, development, and recapitulation built on the tension between two key areas. This logic organized the standardized four-movement symphony, the string quartet, and the sonata. Franz Joseph Haydn did more than any other composer to fix these genres, earning him the labels father of the symphony and of the string quartet through decades of inventive output at the Esterházy court.
terms.example: Haydn's London symphonies (1791–95), such as the 'Surprise', show the mature Classical style: witty thematic development, a sudden fortissimo chord to jolt the listener, and a fully formed four-movement design.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Charles Rosen, The Classical Style; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'sonata form'

terms.short: The recent shift to digital capture, computer-generated imagery, and on-demand streaming distribution that reshaped how films are made and seen.
terms.definition: From the 1990s onward, digital technology overturned both production and distribution. Computer-generated imagery and digital compositing made photoreal impossibilities routine, and digital cameras and projection displaced photochemical film as the industry standard. Distribution shifted again as streaming platforms moved viewing from theaters into homes and onto personal screens, funding original films and series at scale and compressing or bypassing the theatrical window. These changes lowered some production barriers, globalized audiences, and unsettled long-standing release models, raising fresh questions about the cinema experience itself.
terms.example: James Cameron's Avatar (2009), built on performance capture and a fully digital 3-D world, exemplified how computer-generated imagery could render an entire alien planet — a spectacle impossible to stage photochemically.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; British Film Institute (BFI); The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: The nonfiction lineage of cinema, from staged actuality to observational movements claiming a fresh access to reality.
terms.definition: Documentary runs parallel to fiction film from cinema's start and continually redefines its claim on truth. Robert Flaherty's Nanook of the North dramatized and partly staged Inuit life, while Dziga Vertov's kino-eye reassembled real footage into a portrait of the modern city. Lighter, portable sound and camera technology in the 1960s enabled cinéma vérité, which provoked and participated in events, and American direct cinema, which sought to observe unobtrusively as a 'fly on the wall.' These movements debated how much a camera shapes the reality it records — a question still central to nonfiction.
terms.example: The American direct-cinema landmark Primary (1960), trailing John F. Kennedy through a campaign with handheld cameras and synchronous sound, showed how new lightweight gear let filmmakers seem to simply observe events as they unfolded.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; Bill Nichols, Introduction to Documentary; The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: Roughly 500–1400: a Christianised, symbolic art of chant, icon, illuminated manuscript, and Gothic verticality.
terms.definition: After Rome's fall the arts reorganised around the Church and the court. Meaning ran through symbol and hierarchy rather than naturalism: gold-ground Byzantine icons, illuminated manuscripts, and soaring Gothic cathedrals expressed the sacred, while Gregorian chant and the first written polyphony built the grammar of Western notation. Vernacular literature — chivalric romance, Dante, Chaucer — began to rival Latin. Giotto's turn toward weight and feeling near the period's end seeds the Renaissance to come.
terms.example: A single illuminated Book of Hours fuses three arts at once — painting (miniatures), literature (devotional text), and the chant it accompanied — showing how the medieval arts served one liturgical whole.
terms.source: Janson's History of Art (Medieval art); Taruskin, Oxford History of Western Music (chant & early polyphony); Encyclopædia Britannica (Middle Ages)

terms.short: The early-20th-century novel that broke linear narrative to render the flow of consciousness.
terms.definition: The modernist novel of the early 20th century abandoned the orderly plots of realism to capture the fragmented, subjective experience of time and mind. James Joyce's Ulysses mapped a single Dublin day through dense allusion and shifting styles, climaxing in Molly Bloom's unpunctuated interior monologue; Virginia Woolf dissolved external action into the rippling inner lives of Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse. Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time built an immense architecture of involuntary memory. These writers developed stream of consciousness and free indirect discourse to follow thought as it actually moves.
terms.example: In Proust's novel, the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea suddenly resurrects the narrator's entire childhood — a single sensation unspooling involuntary memory and setting the book's whole method of recovering lost time.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The 19th-century novel of detailed social observation and psychological depth.
terms.definition: The realist novel dominated 19th-century fiction by rendering contemporary society with documentary detail and moral seriousness. In England, Charles Dickens dramatized industrial and urban life across vast casts, while George Eliot brought philosophical and psychological depth to provincial communities in Middlemarch. In France, Gustave Flaubert pursued exact prose and ironic distance in Madame Bovary; in Russia, Leo Tolstoy achieved panoramic scope and intimate consciousness in War and Peace and Anna Karenina. Realism treated ordinary lives as worthy of epic attention and refined free indirect style to enter characters' minds.
terms.example: Flaubert spends pages on the layered structure of Emma Bovary's wedding cake and her provincial boredom, building a meticulously observed world whose very ordinariness exposes the gap between her romantic dreams and her life.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of World Literature; The Oxford Companion to English Literature; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: ~1400–1600: the rebirth of classical learning, linear perspective, humanism, and the individual artist.
terms.definition: Centred on Italy and spreading north, the Renaissance recovered classical antiquity and fused it with empirical observation. Linear perspective gave painting measured depth; humanism placed the human individual at the centre of literature and learning; Josquin and Palestrina perfected vocal polyphony; courtly dance was codified; and dress became a deliberate statement of status and proportion. The era invents the modern idea of the named, virtuoso artist — Leonardo, Michelangelo, Shakespeare, Cervantes — whose work is signed achievement, not anonymous craft.
terms.example: Brunelleschi's demonstration of one-point perspective is a hinge for the whole period: a geometric trick in painting that mirrors the era's wider move toward a measured, human-scaled, rationally ordered world.
terms.source: Gombrich, The Story of Art (Renaissance); Grove Art Online (Renaissance); Encyclopædia Britannica (Renaissance)

terms.short: The 18th-century emergence of the realist English novel as a popular literary form.
terms.definition: In early 18th-century England the novel emerged as a sustained prose narrative of ordinary individual lives, addressed to a growing middle-class readership. Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe and Moll Flanders offered circumstantial, first-person realism; Samuel Richardson's epistolary Pamela and Clarissa pioneered intimate psychological interiority through letters; Henry Fielding answered with the panoramic comic plotting of Tom Jones. Critic Ian Watt linked this 'rise of the novel' to economic individualism and a new premium on particularity and probability. The form's conventions of character, plot, and verisimilitude shaped fiction ever after.
terms.example: Defoe's Robinson Crusoe inventories his salvaged tools and tallies days on a calendar post — an accumulation of practical detail that taught readers to believe a fictional life because it was documented like a real one.
terms.source: The Norton Anthology of English Literature; Ian Watt, The Rise of the Novel; Encyclopædia Britannica

terms.short: The 19th-century symphony grew in size, color, and narrative ambition, split between program music and absolute form.
terms.definition: After Beethoven, Romantic composers expanded the orchestra and the emotional scope of the symphony, exploiting a larger palette of instruments and bolder harmony for heightened expression. One path was program music, instrumental works that tell a story or evoke images, pioneered by Hector Berlioz, whose vivid orchestration and recurring melodic idée fixe pushed the form toward literary narrative. A countercurrent upheld absolute music, symphonies valued as pure form, championed by Johannes Brahms, who absorbed Beethoven's legacy while resisting overt programs. The era also produced the tone poem and ever-larger forces.
terms.example: Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830) depicts an artist's opium-fueled obsession across five movements, with a recurring beloved-theme transformed grotesquely into a witches' sabbath in the finale.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Richard Taruskin, The Oxford History of Western Music, vol. 3; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'program music'

terms.short: The first decades of cinema (~1895–1929) in which the medium invented its own visual grammar before synchronized sound.
terms.definition: Cinema began with the Lumière brothers' actuality films and Georges Méliès's trick-film fantasies, then matured as filmmakers discovered editing, the close-up, and parallel action. D.W. Griffith consolidated this grammar into a fluent narrative language with crosscutting and intertitles, while the comedians Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton turned mime and physical timing into a universal art. With no dialogue, meaning was carried entirely by image, gesture, framing, and live musical accompaniment. By the late 1920s the basic vocabulary of shots and cuts that all later cinema would build on was already in place.
terms.example: Buster Keaton's Sherlock Jr. (1924) — in which his projectionist literally walks into the movie screen — crystallizes how silent filmmakers used purely visual invention, stunt, and editing to tell a story without a spoken word.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; British Film Institute (BFI); The Oxford History of World Cinema

terms.short: The Delft master of quiet interiors bathed in luminous, carefully observed daylight.
terms.definition: Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) of Delft painted a small body of mostly domestic interiors notable for their serene composition and exquisite rendering of natural light falling across walls, fabrics, and faces. He observed optical effects with extraordinary care — soft highlights, the diffusion of color in shadow, the texture of surfaces — and may have studied projected images through a camera obscura. His restrained palette, balanced geometry, and stilled, often solitary figures lend ordinary moments a contemplative monumentality. Largely forgotten after his death, he was rediscovered in the nineteenth century and is now ranked among the greatest of Dutch painters. His work epitomizes the Golden Age's attention to perception and the everyday.
terms.example: Girl with a Pearl Earring (c. 1665) isolates a turning girl against a dark ground, the soft daylight catching her parted lips and the single luminous highlight on the pearl, with no narrative beyond the charged glance.
terms.source: Gardner's Art Through the Ages; Gombrich, The Story of Art; Grove Art Online; The Met Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History

terms.short: Nineteenth-century dress that re-corseted the body and reshaped the skirt through successive engineered silhouettes.
terms.definition: Victorian women's dress returned to the tightly corseted waist and built ever-changing skirt structures around it. The cage crinoline of the 1850s–60s used hooped steel to support enormous bell skirts without layers of heavy petticoats; later the bustle shifted volume to the back. Industrialization transformed the trade — mechanized weaving, the sewing machine, synthetic aniline dyes, and the department store made fashionable cloth and clothing cheaper and more available. Dress codes were elaborate and strictly gendered, with mourning dress, day and evening dress, and respectability all minutely regulated.
terms.example: The cage crinoline, patented in the 1850s, let one steel-hooped underskirt replace many petticoats — an industrial-age engineering solution that ballooned skirts to their widest extent before the bustle took over.
terms.source: Valerie Steele (ed.), The Berg Companion to Fashion; The Met Costume Institute / Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History; Encyclopædia Britannica ("dress, Western")

terms.short: The prodigy who brought the Classical style to its most fluent and dramatic perfection across every genre.
terms.definition: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart absorbed the Classical idiom and pushed it to a peak of melodic grace, formal balance, and dramatic depth. A child prodigy turned freelance Viennese composer, he wrote with apparent effortlessness in every genre of his time: symphonies, concertos, chamber music, sacred works, and above all opera. He fused Italian lyricism with German contrapuntal craft and gave instrumental music a new expressive range, while his operas drew vivid, humane characters through music. His late works deepen Classical clarity with chromatic richness that points toward Romanticism.
terms.example: The opera Don Giovanni (1787) blends comedy and tragedy, ending with the title character dragged to hell by a stone statue over some of the most dramatically charged orchestral writing of the century.
terms.source: The Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (Oxford); Maynard Solomon, Mozart: A Life; Encyclopædia Britannica, 'Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart'

terms.short: The global tradition of major national art cinemas whose masters expanded film's formal and cultural range beyond Hollywood.
terms.definition: Across the mid-twentieth century, filmmakers outside the Hollywood orbit built distinct national cinemas of the highest artistic ambition. Japan's Akira Kurosawa brought dynamic staging and humanist epics to international screens, while Yasujirō Ozu refined a quiet, low-camera style of domestic life; Sweden's Ingmar Bergman probed faith and psyche in austere chamber dramas; and India's Satyajit Ray rendered Bengali life with lyric realism. Carried by the postwar festival circuit, these bodies of work proved cinema a fully serious art with many centers, influencing filmmakers everywhere.
terms.example: Kurosawa's Rashomon (1950), recounting one crime through four irreconcilable testimonies, stunned the Venice festival and opened Western audiences to Japanese cinema as an equal of any national tradition.
terms.source: Bordwell & Thompson, Film History: An Introduction; The Oxford History of World Cinema; British Film Institute (BFI) Sight and Sound
